description: Pathogens, the immune response, vaccination, antibiotics and monoclonal antibodies.
content_html:
Health, Disease and Pathogens

Health is a state of complete physical and mental well-being, not merely the absence of disease. Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens — microorganisms including bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists. These are spread by direct contact, airborne droplets, contaminated food or water, or animal vectors such as mosquitoes. Non-communicable diseases cannot be transmitted between people. Examples include cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, cancer and asthma. Risk factors include smoking, poor diet, physical inactivity and obesity — though genetic factors also play a role.

Different pathogens cause disease through different mechanisms. Bacteria reproduce rapidly inside the body and release toxins that damage cells and tissues. Viruses invade host cells, hijack their genetic machinery to replicate, and burst out of the cell (lysis), destroying it. Fungi can cause surface infections (e.g. athlete’s foot) or systemic infections in individuals with weakened immunity. Protists include Plasmodium, which causes malaria and is transmitted by mosquito vectors.

Key Fact

Pathogens (bacteria, viruses, fungi, protists) cause communicable diseases by different mechanisms. Non-communicable diseases (cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancer) are linked to lifestyle and genetic risk factors and cannot spread between people.

The Body’s Defence Systems

The body has several lines of defence against pathogens. Non-specific defences (first line) prevent pathogens from entering:

• Skin — a physical barrier that prevents most pathogens from entering unless broken.
• Mucus and cilia in the respiratory tract — mucus traps pathogens; cilia sweep the mucus up and out of the airways.
• Stomach acid (approximately pH 2) — kills most pathogens ingested with food or water.
• Tears and saliva — contain the enzyme lysozyme, which breaks down bacterial cell walls.

If pathogens get past these barriers, the inflammatory response is triggered. Damaged cells release chemicals that cause blood vessels to dilate and become more permeable, increasing blood flow to the infected area (causing redness and warmth) and allowing white blood cells to migrate into the tissue more rapidly.

If pathogens breach the non-specific defences, the specific immune response is activated. Each pathogen carries unique proteins on its surface called antigens. B lymphocytes recognise foreign antigens and produce antibodies — Y-shaped proteins that bind specifically to the matching antigen. Antibodies work by clumping pathogens together (agglutination) for easier destruction, neutralising toxins, and marking pathogens for engulfment by phagocytes.

T lymphocytes work alongside B lymphocytes. T lymphocytes recognise and destroy body cells that have been infected by viruses or bacteria, preventing further spread. They also activate B lymphocytes to produce antibodies. After infection, some lymphocytes become memory cells that persist in the body for years. If the same pathogen is encountered again, memory cells trigger a much faster and larger antibody response, usually preventing illness entirely.

Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens through a process called phagocytosis. This is a non-specific response — phagocytes target any foreign material, not just specific pathogens.

Key Fact

B lymphocytes produce antibodies specific to antigens. T lymphocytes destroy infected cells and activate B lymphocytes. Memory cells enable a faster response to reinfection. Phagocytes engulf pathogens non-specifically.

Vaccination and Antibiotics

Vaccination introduces a harmless form of a pathogen — which may be dead, weakened, or just its antigens — into the body. The immune system responds by producing antibodies and memory cells, without causing the disease. If the real pathogen enters later, memory cells trigger a rapid response. Mass vaccination programmes have dramatically reduced or eliminated diseases such as smallpox, measles, polio and tetanus in many countries.

Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or stop them reproducing. They target structures that bacteria have but human cells lack, such as the bacterial cell wall. This makes them selectively toxic — harmful to bacteria but safe for human cells. Importantly, antibiotics do not work against viruses, because viruses lack the cellular structures that antibiotics target and instead use the host cell’s own machinery to replicate. Overuse and misuse of antibiotics drives antibiotic resistance, producing strains that are very difficult to treat.

Monoclonal antibodies are produced by fusing a specific B lymphocyte (that produces the desired antibody) with a tumour cell to create a hybridoma cell. Hybridoma cells can be grown indefinitely in culture and will continuously produce large quantities of identical antibodies, all specific to the same antigen. Because they are identical and highly specific, monoclonal antibodies can be engineered to target a particular protein or cell type with great precision.

Uses of monoclonal antibodies include:
• Pregnancy tests — detecting the hormone hCG in urine.
• Cancer diagnosis and therapy — antibodies tagged with a radioactive marker or drug are delivered directly to tumour cells carrying the target antigen, destroying the cancer cells while sparing healthy tissue.
• Blood tests — detecting specific proteins or pathogens in blood samples.
• Autoimmune disease treatment — blocking immune signals that cause conditions like rheumatoid arthritis.

Monoclonal antibodies offer greater precision than many conventional drug treatments but side effects remain a concern — the immune system sometimes reacts to the introduced antibody proteins. Research into new applications is ongoing.

Key Fact

Monoclonal antibodies are produced from hybridoma cells (B lymphocyte + tumour cell). They are highly specific and used in pregnancy tests, cancer treatment, blood tests and autoimmune disease therapy.
exam_tip_html: For immune response questions, make sure you distinguish between specific and non-specific defences. Phagocytosis is non-specific (works against any pathogen); antibody production by lymphocytes is specific (one antibody shape per antigen). For antibiotic questions, a common error is stating that antibiotics kill viruses — they do not: antibiotics target bacterial cell walls and other bacterial structures that viruses lack. For vaccination questions, always mention memory cells as the basis for long-term immunity, not just antibodies (antibody levels decline, but memory cells persist). For monoclonal antibody questions (Higher tier), you need to describe the hybridoma cell production process and name at least two specific uses.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Pathogens (bacteria, viruses, fungi, protists) cause communicable diseases by releasing toxins or destroying cells. Non-communicable diseases such as cardiovascular disease and cancer are linked to lifestyle and genetic risk factors and cannot spread between people.
  • The immune system responds through non-specific defences (skin, mucus, stomach acid) and specific responses (B lymphocytes produce antibodies, T lymphocytes destroy infected cells). Memory cells allow a faster response to reinfection. Vaccination exploits this memory without causing disease.
  • Antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses; overuse drives antibiotic resistance. Monoclonal antibodies (Higher tier) are produced from hybridoma cells and used in pregnancy tests, cancer treatment and blood tests.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly explains why antibiotics are effective against bacteria but not viruses?
A) Bacteria are larger than viruses
B) Antibiotics target bacterial cell walls, which viruses lack
C) Viruses are destroyed by the immune system before antibiotics reach them
D) Antibiotics only work in the bloodstream, where viruses do not travel
practice_questions.marks: B) Antibiotics target bacterial cell walls, which viruses lack [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the names of two types of white blood cell involved in the specific immune response.
practice_questions.marks: B lymphocytes AND T lymphocytes [1 mark for both — accept phagocytes as a third type if the student lists three and the correct two are included]

practice_questions.text: Describe how vaccination protects an individual against future infection.
practice_questions.marks: A dead, weakened or inactivated form of the pathogen is introduced into the body [1 mark]; the immune system produces antibodies and memory cells so that if the real pathogen enters, a faster and larger immune response destroys it before illness develops [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between communicable and non-communicable diseases. Give one example of each.
practice_questions.marks: Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens and can be passed from one organism to another [1 mark]; non-communicable diseases cannot be spread between individuals and are caused by lifestyle, genetic or environmental factors [1 mark]; example of communicable: any valid pathogen-caused disease (e.g. influenza, cholera, malaria); example of non-communicable: any valid example (e.g. cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, cancer) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain the role of B lymphocytes, antibodies and memory cells in protecting the body from a pathogen it has encountered before.
practice_questions.marks: B lymphocytes recognise the foreign antigens on the pathogen and produce specific antibodies that bind to them, marking the pathogen for destruction [1 mark]; memory cells formed during the first infection persist in the body for years [1 mark]; on reinfection, memory cells rapidly produce large quantities of the specific antibody, destroying the pathogen before it can cause illness [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of monoclonal antibodies in cancer treatment, considering both their advantages and limitations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate explanation of how monoclonal antibodies are produced and how they target cancer; balanced evaluation of advantages and limitations; justified conclusion.
Secure: Correct production method described; at least two advantages and one limitation; conclusion present.
Developing: Some correct content; one-sided evaluation; limited development.
Emerging: Vague description; few relevant points.

Points may include:
Production: B lymphocyte fused with tumour cell to form hybridoma; hybridoma cultured to produce large quantities of identical antibodies specific to the cancer cell antigen.
Advantages: highly specific to cancer cell antigen, reducing damage to healthy tissue; can be tagged with radioactive substances, drugs or toxins to deliver treatment directly to the tumour; used in diagnosis (detecting cancer markers in blood).
Limitations: can cause immune reactions as the body may respond to the introduced antibody proteins; expensive to produce; not effective against all cancer types; still relatively new technology with side effects still being researched.
Conclusion should weigh the precision advantage against the limitations.

knowledge_checks.q: What do B lymphocytes produce to help fight a specific pathogen?
Why do memory cells allow a faster immune response on second infection?
options: They remain in the body and rapidly produce the specific antibody when the pathogen returns
They strengthen the skin barrier against pathogens

knowledge_checks.q: Antibiotics are effective against bacteria because they target bacterial cell _____, which human cells do not have.
Vaccination works by introducing a dead or weakened pathogen so the immune system produces antibodies and _____ cells for future protection.
Match each defence to its description:
right: Non-specific engulfing and digestion of pathogens
Produce antibodies specific to a pathogen's antigens
Destroy infected cells and activate B lymphocytes
Persist after infection to enable a faster future response

flashcard_questions.a: A microorganism that invades a host and causes disease (bacteria, virus, fungus or protist).

flashcard_questions.q: How do bacteria cause disease differently from viruses?
flashcard_questions.a: Bacteria produce toxins; viruses hijack host cells and destroy them when replicating.
Proteins on the surface of a pathogen that trigger an immune response.
Antibodies specific to a pathogen's antigens.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of T lymphocytes?
flashcard_questions.a: They destroy infected cells and activate B lymphocytes.

flashcard_questions.q: What are memory cells and why do they matter?
flashcard_questions.a: Long-lived lymphocytes that allow a faster antibody response on reinfection.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do antibiotics not work against viruses?
flashcard_questions.a: Viruses lack the bacterial cell wall and structures that antibiotics target.

flashcard_questions.q: How does vaccination produce immunity without causing disease?
flashcard_questions.a: A harmless form of the pathogen stimulates antibody and memory cell production.

flashcard_questions.q: What are monoclonal antibodies produced from? (Higher Tier)
flashcard_questions.a: Hybridoma cells — formed by fusing a B lymphocyte with a tumour cell.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two medical uses of monoclonal antibodies. (Higher Tier)
flashcard_questions.a: Pregnancy testing (detecting hCG) and targeted cancer treatment.
The non-specific process by which phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens.

glossary_terms.definition: Diseases caused by microorganisms (pathogens) that can spread from one host to another through various routes.
Microorganisms that invade a host organism and cause disease, including bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists.
Diseases that cannot spread between individuals, caused by factors such as lifestyle, genetics or environmental exposure.
Proteins on the surface of a pathogen recognised as foreign by the immune system, triggering an immune response.
White blood cells that produce antibodies specific to a particular antigen.
Y-shaped proteins produced by B lymphocytes that bind to specific antigens on pathogens, marking them for destruction.
White blood cells that destroy infected cells directly and activate B lymphocytes during the specific immune response.
The process by which phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens or debris, forming a non-specific defence.
Introducing a dead, weakened or inactive form of a pathogen (or its antigens) into the body to stimulate the immune system to produce memory cells and antibodies, providing future immunity.
When bacteria evolve through natural selection to survive exposure to antibiotics, making infections harder to treat.
Identical antibodies produced from a single clone of B lymphocytes (hybridoma cells), all specific to the same antigen. Used in medical testing and treatment.
